caption: John explicitly connects Jesus’s unbroken bones with Scripture. It is precise Passover typology, but Numbers originally gives a rule for preparing a meal.

slides.alt_text: Editorial slide: Jesus’s bones were not broken Numbers says a Passover animal’s bones must remain unbroken. John says soldiers left Jesus’s legs intact and calls it fulfilment.
slides.body: Numbers says a Passover animal’s bones must remain unbroken. John says soldiers left Jesus’s legs intact and calls it fulfilment.
slides.heading: Jesus’s bones were not broken

slides.alt_text: The BSB text of Num 9:12: they may not leave any of it until morning or break any of its bones.
slides.body: they may not leave any of it until morning or break any of its bones.
slides.heading: Num 9:12

slides.alt_text: The claimed New Testament fulfilment in Jn 19:33, 36, BSB: They did not break His legs. Now these things happened so that the Scripture would be fulfilled: ‘Not one of His bones will be broken.’
slides.body: They did not break His legs. Now these things happened so that the Scripture would be fulfilled: ‘Not one of His bones will be broken.’
slides.heading: Claimed fulfilment · Jn 19:33, 36

slides.alt_text: Editorial slide: John makes the connection The detail is unusually exact. John presents Jesus as a Passover sacrifice whose bones remain unbroken.
slides.body: The detail is unusually exact. John presents Jesus as a Passover sacrifice whose bones remain unbroken.
slides.heading: John makes the connection

slides.alt_text: Editorial slide: But Numbers gives a meal rule Numbers tells people how to prepare a Passover animal. It does not predict an execution. John gives the old rule a Christian meaning.
slides.body: Numbers tells people how to prepare a Passover animal. It does not predict an execution. John gives the old rule a Christian meaning.
slides.heading: But Numbers gives a meal rule

title: Not one bone broken
